You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: US Market Shift: From "Compute" to "Storage," Up 764% in 6 Months! S&P 500 Top 10 Revealed: AI Storage Chain Dominates, Q2 Hits 4-Year High.

TEXT:
I. Q2 Explosion: S&P 500 Delivers Strongest Quarterly Performance Since 2020
The S&P 500 rose approximately 9% in the first half of the year. Although geopolitical tensions (related to Iran) caused volatility in Q1, the index rebounded strongly in Q2 with a quarterly gain of around 15%—its best performance since 2020. The index successfully breached key psychological barriers at 7,000 and 7,500 points, signaling a significant回暖 in market confidence.
Broadly speaking, 62% of constituent stocks posted positive returns. This rally was not driven by a handful of mega-caps but featured broader market participation compared previous highly concentrated trends.
In short, this performance was fueled by better-than-expected corporate earnings and substantial upward revisions to EPS forecasts by analysts, rather than mere speculative sentiment.
II. Clear Driving Logic: AI Data Center "Storage Power" Demand Skyrockets Storage and Hardware Stocks
Unlike the previous rally led by Mag7 software giants, this wave of gains was concentrated in the underlying hardware infrastructure of AI, particularly storage, memory, and supporting equipment. As AI model training, inference, and practical applications require massive data access, storage speed and capacity have become critical bottlenecks, leading to a collective surge in related stocks.
The top ten performers were dominated by IT and tech stocks:
SanDisk ( SNDK ): +764% (Enterprise SSD market share rose to 8%; triple-level and quad-level cell memory technologies landed)
Micron ( MU ): +301%
Western Digital ( WDC ): +278%
Intel ( INTC ): +257%
Seagate ( STX ): +252%
Dell ( DELL ): +229%
Marvell ( MRVL ): +227%
Followed by Applied Materials ( AMAT ): +170% and Lumentum ( LITE ): +131%.
While the previous cycle chased GPU computing power, this round saw a catch-up surge across the entire supply chain—including memory, SSDs, HDDs, servers, and semiconductor equipment—with profit expectations significantly revised upward (e.g., SanDisk’s EPS forecast was上调 nearly 10-fold). Beyond the storage chain, the energy sector also performed strongly due to geopolitical factors, becoming one of the best-performing sectors in H1.
III. Key Catalysts Investors Are Watching in H2
Market focus in the second half will center on several key issues:
Q2 Earnings Season: Kicking off in mid-to-late July, can these AI hardware companies continue to deliver impressive numbers and validate the sustainability of demand?
Hyperscaler Capex: Will tech giants like Microsoft , Google, Amazon , and Meta maintain high-intensity AI capital expenditure plans, or will there be marginal slowdowns?
Infrastructure Bottlenecks: Can power supply, cooling systems, and supply chain constraints facing large-scale data center construction be effectively resolved? These issues may cap growth potential.
Additionally, macroeconomic data (such as employment and inflation), the Federal Reserve’s interest rate path, and broader evidence of AI implementation and ROI in enterprise settings will directly impact risk appetite.
Overall, although valuations have been partially digested by earnings revisions (S&P 500 forward P/E is approx. 20.3), structural opportunities within the AI theme remain. It is advisable to focus on supply chain stocks with high order visibility and solid fundamentals, while avoiding pure concept speculation.
Summary
The market’s real gains in the first half tell us that AI has moved from the conceptual stage to a period of tangible infrastructure investment. The storage and semiconductor equipment chains have emerged as the biggest winners due to explosive rigid demand.
While short-term volatility remains inevitable (due to geopolitics, macro data, etc.), supply chain opportunities driven by technological progress are worth tracking for the medium to long term.
Investors are advised to monitor these themes dynamically according to their risk preferences to capture structural market opportunities!
